reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Bolognia Dermatology
clinicalPearls: An umbrella group of disorders defined by abnormal accumulation of mucin (glycosaminoglycans, chiefly hyaluronic acid) in the dermis or hair follicles, produced by fibroblasts
Broadly divided into primary mucinoses, where mucin deposition is the defining pathology, and secondary mucinoses, where mucin is an incidental finding in another disease such as lupus erythematosus

Primary degenerative-inflammatory forms include lichen myxoedematosus and scleromyxoedema, scleroedema, reticular erythematous mucinosis, self-healing juvenile cutaneous mucinosis and papular mucinosis
Pretibial myxoedema (thyroid dermopathy) is a distinctive form seen in Graves disease, driven by thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies, presenting as firm plaques and nodules over the shins

Follicular mucinosis (alopecia mucinosa) shows mucin within hair follicles and may be idiopathic or a marker of mycosis fungoides, so persistent or atypical lesions warrant exclusion of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
Investigation combines biopsy with mucin stains (Alcian blue, colloidal iron) and a search for associations such as thyroid disease, paraproteinaemia and connective tissue disease
Management is directed at the specific subtype and any underlying disorder, since prognosis and treatment differ widely across the group
reference.pathophysiology: The cutaneous mucinoses share deposition of mucin, a jelly-like mixture of acid glycosaminoglycans (predominantly hyaluronic acid) secreted by dermal fibroblasts, within the connective tissue or, in follicular mucinosis, within the follicular epithelium. In many primary forms, fibroblasts are stimulated to overproduce glycosaminoglycans by circulating factors: paraproteins in scleromyxoedema, thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies and other cytokines in pretibial myxoedema, and immune or inflammatory mediators in reticular erythematous mucinosis and lupus-associated disease. Accumulated hyaluronic acid is hygroscopic and separates collagen bundles, producing the induration, papules, plaques or oedematous changes characteristic of each subtype. In follicular mucinosis, mucin accumulates between keratinocytes of the follicle, sometimes in association with a lymphomatous infiltrate.
additionalDifferentials: Pretibial myxoedema and generalised myxoedema of hypothyroidism
Reticular erythematous mucinosis and lupus erythematosus tumidus
Follicular mucinosis with or without mycosis fungoides
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with Alcian blue or colloidal iron staining to confirm and localise mucin
Thyroid function tests and thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies where pretibial myxoedema is suspected
Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to detect a paraprotein
Autoimmune serology when a connective tissue disease is considered
Assessment for cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, including clonality studies, in persistent follicular mucinosis
Investigations tailored to the suspected specific subtype and its systemic associations
redFlags: Follicular mucinosis with atypical or persistent lesions suggesting underlying mycosis fungoides
Widespread papular mucinosis with a paraprotein indicating scleromyxoedema and possible systemic involvement
Neurological, cardiac or gastrointestinal features accompanying a sclerodermoid mucinosis
Rapid progression or systemic symptoms prompting evaluation for an associated systemic disorder
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies greatly by subtype: self-healing juvenile cutaneous mucinosis and post-infectious scleroedema may resolve, pretibial myxoedema and macular forms are usually chronic but benign, whereas scleromyxoedema and lymphoma-associated follicular mucinosis carry the potential for serious systemic disease. Outcome depends on accurate subtyping and management of the underlying condition.
pitfalls: Treating all mucinoses as a single entity rather than identifying the specific subtype, which determines prognosis and therapy
Missing an associated systemic disorder such as thyroid disease, paraproteinaemia or connective tissue disease
Failing to exclude mycosis fungoides in persistent follicular mucinosis
Overlooking mucin as a secondary clue to lupus erythematosus or other connective tissue disease
Relying on routine histology without specific mucin stains, so that subtle dermal mucin is missed
